title: Arignar Anna's 'Neethi Devan Mayakkam': Classical Satire and Courtroom Logic (1947)
summary: In his landmark theatrical masterpiece Neethi Devan Mayakkam (The Delusion of the God of Justice), C. N. Annadurai used stunning courtroom rhetoric to challenge classical double standards.
full_text:
In 1947, across the dramatic stages of Tamil Nadu, C. N. Annadurai's political and philosophical play, Neethi Devan Mayakkam ('The Delusion of the God of Justice'), caused an intellectual earthquake.

The climax of the play takes place in the celestial courtroom of the God of Justice (Dharmaraja), where the mythological king of Lanka, Ravana, is put on trial for abducting Sita. Anna himself frequently performed on stage, acting as the defense advocate for the condemned monarch.

The prosecuting counsel thundered: "Ravana is an incorrigible monster who abducted the virtuous Princess of Ayodhya! Justice demands he be condemned to eternal damnation!"

Anna rose, clad in the black robes of a defense advocate, his voice cutting through the celestial hall with magnificent cadence:
"Lord Justice, I do not deny that Ravana abducted Sita. But can this court render true justice without examining the genesis of the tragedy?
When Ravana's sister Surpanakha approached the royal brothers in the Panchavati forest, what was her crime? Was it a capital offense that Lakshmana should draw his sword and brutally mutilate her nose and ears? By what canon of jurisprudence was that savagery justified against an unarmed woman?

Enraged by the horrific mutilation of his sister, a grieving brother retaliated by abducting Sita. Yet even in his vengeance, did he lay a single dishonorable finger upon her? No! He housed her with royal reverence in the Ashoka grove, guarding her honor intact.
Those who maimed a woman’s body are celebrated as paragons of virtue, while the king who retaliated but guarded a woman’s modesty is branded a demon for eternity! Is this impartial justice, or the blind delusion of prejudice?"

The sheer rhetorical audacity and logical rigor of Anna's dialogue drew thunderous ovations. Through theater, Anna transformed classical mythology into a critical forum for social justice and rational scrutiny.
